column4: The observer is told to look at his food and drink, his donkey, and the animal’s bones as God raises and clothes them; it joins commanded looking, provision, animal anatomy, and creation as evidence of resurrection.
People are commanded to travel through the earth and observe how God began creation, uniting the camel’s function as a means of travel with the section’s command to look at how it was created.
Disbelievers eat as livestock eat before the Fire becomes their dwelling; this reverses the section’s modestly sufficient camel by showing humans consuming without understanding or saving themselves.
People who neither hear nor reason are likened to livestock and judged further astray, a pointed reversal of the section’s expectation that a human should look at the camel and learn from it.
Joseph is asked about seven fat cows consumed by seven lean ones, repeating the animal-fat image of 12:43 while explicitly seeking its meaning for the coming abundance and famine.
Honoring God’s ritual symbols is traced to the piety of hearts; this supplies the inward stance for the sacrificial animals called divine symbols in 22:36.
The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial offerings, and their garlands are made a support for people, placing the camel offering within the institutions that sustain pilgrimage life.
Gardens and springs form part of Thamud’s secure abundance in the speech that soon introduces the she-camel, supplying the water-rich setting against which her allotted drink matters.
Crops and laden palms add pasture and food abundance to the same Thamud setting before the she-camel’s water share is imposed.
Thamud carve skillful houses from mountains in the she-camel passage; these fixed stone dwellings contrast with the portable houses the section says livestock skins provide.

Immediately after the she-camel warning, Thamud are reminded of palaces on the plain and homes carved in mountains; their fixed architecture illuminates by contrast the camel-skin dwelling carried through a journey.
Paradise attendants carry goblets, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing spring, extending the section’s meeting between a milk-giving camel, cups filled in sequence, and the furnished Garden.
The tree of Zaqqum begins another Qur’anic hell-food scene, a fire-grown counterpart to the source dictionary’s ordinary fodder plant called “camel bread.”
Zaqqum is identified as the sinner’s food, turning a plant into punishment rather than the small amount of herbage that sustains the camel.

The hypocrites would have followed for near gain and an easy journey, but the distance seemed too great; that failed journey clarifies why the camel’s ability to carry people far is a consequential provision.
Human creation and the animals God disperses are signs for people of certainty, directly generalizing the invited gaze at the camel as a created sign.
Every land animal is described as belonging to communities like humans, adding a creaturely social dimension to the camel herd beyond its value as property.
The sheep and goat pairs begin the enumeration completed by camels and cattle in 6:144, locating the camel pair within the full created livestock set rather than in isolation.
Mountains become like wool on the last day, bringing the distant mountain together with the animal fiber that the section says supplies furnishings and portable homes.
Mountains become like fluffed wool, a repeated judgment-day reversal in which the fixed object set opposite the camel takes on the appearance of livestock fiber.
A human has only what he strives for, giving moral consequence to س ع ي while the source section’s dictionary branch uses the root for a moderate physical run within the camel journey.

The “great sacrifice” that ransoms Abraham’s son plausibly belongs beside the camel offerings of 22:33–37 as another divinely provided sacrificial animal, though this ayah itself does not name its species.
